item.title: Tinker, tailor, soldier ... tech boss?
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang? • Why is Nvidia so powerful in the AI world, and what could Jensen Huang’s scandal really cost? • Nvidia, Jensen Huang and the history of ‘sexpionage’ • El Salvador is exporting the ‘Bukele model’ to Haiti – but the gang offensive is a gamble for both nations • Ukraine peace talks end with no breakthrough – but Europe may be set to return from the cold • ‘Plenty of reasons for hope’: what 30 years of climate talks have achieved
item.content:encoded:
Fans of John le Carré will know that a new novel featuring his most enduring character, spymaster George Smiley, dropped this month.

Written by the late author’s son, Nick Harkaway, it is partially set in the U.S. – where, this week, a spy drama of its own was playing out.

On Thursday, Nvidia boss Jensen Huang stepped down amid reports of two extramarital affairs. One was allegedly with a female executive who reported to him, but the other … well, that is where it gets really interesting. According to U.S. intelligence, that woman, an executive at a Singapore-based tech firm, is in fact a Chinese spy. Beijing has dismissed the claim as “pure fabrication,” but to borrow a phrase made famous by a much earlier sex-and-spying scandal: “Well, they would, wouldn’t they?”

That quote originated from the Profumo Affair – a tale of swinging London, beautiful women, a British politician and a Russian attaché, which Robert Dover, a U.K.-based professor of intelligence and national security, cites as an example as he takes readers into the world of “sexpionage.” Linggong Kong, an expert on U.S.-China relations, goes further back. He explores the age-old Chinese concept of “meiren ji” or “beauty stratagem,” through which rival warlords and state agencies used alluring women – and occasionally men – to ensnare, exploit and compromise powerful men.

Apparently “honey trapping” has been going on for millennia. But why deploy the tactic now, allegedly, and why Huang? Tech expert Andrew Cullen explains that Nvidia, as the world’s biggest supplier of the high-end chips, holds great power as the AI race between China and the U.S. heats up – makings its executives key targets.

Great power rivalries, flawed human beings and an intelligence service having to play catch-up. I wonder what le Carré – and Smiley – would make of it all.

Elsewhere this week, we have been keeping an eye on the latest coming out of the COP 31 climate conference and monitoring events in Haiti, where El Salvador’s strongman leader has sent 2,500 troops as part of anti-gang efforts.

item.title: AI is supercharging fraud
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • AI is supercharging money scams – here’s what you can do to protect yourself • AI chatbots can be a valuable health resource for older adults – if they embrace ‘informed skepticism’ • I don’t want AI in my online search. What options do I have? • ‘Make this face look gay’: AI models alter faces to give people stereotypical ‘gay,’ ‘straight’ or ‘criminal’ features • How deep do AI relationships really go? An expert in attachment theory explains
item.content:encoded:
AI is dramatically boosting fraud – literally in the sense of enabling deepfake audio and video “actors” to convincingly portray victims’ loved ones and bosses. A finance professor explains the scope of the problem, how it’s poised to get worse, and the steps you can take to protect yourself.

AI chatbots have become an appealing way for a growing number of older adults to get health information, given the bots’ convenience and ease of use. But AI chatbot responses require a degree of skepticism, and an information studies researcher has found that older adults are less likely than younger ones to check other sources to verify the accuracy of the information they receive.

Also this week, how to avoid AI in your web searches, what happens when you ask an AI to make a photo of a person “look gay,” and whether people are forming relationships with AI chatbots.

Eric Smalley

Science + Technology Editor

AI is supercharging money scams – here’s what you can do to protect yourself

item.title: The steep political price of high energy costs
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high • Voters rejected data centers in dozens of communities, fueling the narrative that opposition to the AI infrastructure contributed to the 2026 blue wave • When a Walmart closes, what happens to nearby stores? • Changes are coming to Airbnb. Here’s what travellers and hosts need to know • How often should you be working at the office? Here’s what the research suggests • Canada wants to rebuild its manufacturing sector, but it’s losing the immigrant workers it needs
item.content:encoded:
The depth and breadth of the Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections has been described by many analysts as historic. But one factor was no surprise at all: the effect of high energy prices on the incumbent party and president.

Time and again, no matter which party is in power, voters are especially punishing when they have to shell out more at the pump, according to Michael A. Mische of the University of Southern California. And while midterm elections typically swing against the party of the sitting president, the incumbent party loses even more seats in Congress when energy costs soar – even though these prices are largely shaped by global forces.

Going back to President Richard Nixon and the oil crises of the 1970s, Mische explains why this pattern is so entrenched and predictable. “When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally,” he notes. “Voters pay attention to those changes.”

Helen Fessenden

Senior Economy and Business Editor, The Conversation U.S.

Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high

item.title: The big ticket items at climate summit in Turkey
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Yes, the COP climate talks are far from perfect. But they still hold the power for change • The Cop31 climate summit is betting on electrification – but still needs a plan to ditch fossil fuels • 5 ways countries stymie climate negotiations without actually saying ‘no’ • COP 31: West Africa’s climate plans put a price on ruined roads and crops – how to add invisible losses
item.content:encoded:
The world is likely living through its hottest year on record, accompanied by more extreme storms, droughts and destructive flooding.

The damage is why over 40,000 politicians, policy writers, advocates, lobbyists and others with a stake in how the world deals with climate change are pouring into Antalya, Turkey this week for the annual UN climate summit.

World leaders and national negotiators have been meeting like this for over 30 years to try to find solutions to climate change.

In some ways it’s a miracle these talks achieve anything when you consider the sheer number of countries involved and that decisions are made by consensus. Yet they do, writes Wesley Morgan. Many countries have been backing away from the fossil fuels that drive climate change, he writes, and renewable energy use is expanding quickly. Greenhouse emissions are slowing as a result.

At this year’s climate summit, COP31, Morgan and others expect to see a push to electrify homes and vehicles, with a goal of 35% electrification by 2035. Negotiators will have to be careful to ensure that the new power comes from clean sources and not more fossil fuels, write Freddie Daley and Peter Newell. As Shannon Gibson explains, the biggest greenhouse emitting countries have a history of attempting to stymie global progress.

Another big issue will be who should pay for the damage when low-income countries that did little to cause climate change are facing the brunt of the harm, write Olasunkanmi Habeeb Okunola and Susan Ekoh.

The Conversation’s Miki Perkins is in Turkey for the conference. She and our colleagues will be working with experts from around the world to share the success stories and the struggles as COP31 unfolds in the coming weeks.

Stacy Morford

Senior Environment + Energy Editor

Yes, the COP climate talks are far from perfect. But they still hold the power for change

Electrification alone won’t deliver a clean energy transition. Two major challenges remain.

The methods can be subtle but effective at slowing progress, particularly when fossil fuels are involved. Here’s what to watch for as the latest global climate talks get underway.

item.title: Will 'world models' succeed where LLMs fall short?
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Why AI cannot ‘think’ like humans do • AI may quickly generate ideas, but working with people leads to more creative ones • AI agents with friendly faces and adorable bodies can distract you from serious risks • From lab to life: Why translating AI advances to the real world is a major challenge • Are you using AI to study? Here’s how to do it well
item.content:encoded:
By now we know the chatbots we interact with are powered by large language models, which, as impressive as they are, have some inherent limitations. According to some of the leading minds in AI, “world models” will succeed LLMs and bring more humanlike thinking to their training, as two psychologists explain.

Agents are rapidly becoming one of the most important advances in AI, and they’re starting to take shape, sometimes in cute packages. Two scholars of digital technologies write that the disarming marketing of agents – think friendly avatars like Meta Muse and OpenAI’s Dots – can mask some of the more “invasive potential of AI agents,” such as acting without a user’s full consent.

Also this week, why working with people rather than AIs can lead to more creativity, some of the biggest challenges in applying AI in the “real world” outside of computers, and tips on using AI to aid rather than detract from studying.

Martin LaMonica

Director of Editorial Projects and Newsletters

Webinar

Lead Story

Why AI cannot ‘think’ like humans do

‘World models’ are an emerging technology that could help AI systems anticipate what might happen and use that to act. This is not the same as human ‘thinking.’

“World models” are an emerging technology that could help AI systems move closer to human “thinking” by helping them learn to anticipate what might happen and use that prediction to act.

Are you using AI to study? Here’s how to do it well

Luke Rowe, Australian Catholic University

A good principle when studying with artificial intelligence is: think first, use AI second (or, in some cases, not at all).

item.title: What the midterms may mean for wars in Iran, Ukraine
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • What the US midterms result means for the Ukraine war • JD Vance singled out Iran War for midterm rout – he didn’t say what should happen next in conflict • Young men and Latino voters helped drive the Democrats’ blue wave. Why did they abandon Trump? • Climate change is undermining our health and the burden falls heaviest on women • Why Trump, Xi, and Putin can’t carve up the world like the ‘big three’ leaders of 1945 • NASA’s Swift telescope has burned up, months after a robot sent to save it failed – here’s why it’s so hard to boost a satellite
item.content:encoded:
This week saw a seismic shift in the political landscape of the U.S. as voters rebuked the Trump agenda and voted in Democrats to key Senate and House seats across the country.

Vice President JD Vance was in no doubt about what drove the blue wave: frustration over the war in Iran.

Javed Ali, who served as a senior member of the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, believes this prognosis is correct. But he is less sure that Vance, Trump or anyone else in the administration really knows what to do with that knowledge. “America and Iran have both borne significant political, military and economic costs. A decision not to pursue an endgame would leave those sunk; doing so may only increase them,” writes Ali.

And the fact that from January, Donald Trump will have to navigate a Congress controlled by Democrats almost uniformly opposed to the war will give him less leeway to act.

That dynamic may affect the calculus in Washington regarding the conflict in Ukraine, too. “Having just scored a sweeping landslide victory, [Democrats] may well calculate there is a good deal of political mileage to be had now in escalating their attack on a weakened Trump if his foreign policy towards Russia and Ukraine continues … to reward an aggressor while making the victim of that aggression look like an obstacle to a settlement,” notes international relations expert Michael Cox.

Elsewhere today we look forward towards COP31, the U.N. climate conference due to begin on Monday and salute the legacy of NASA’s Swift Observatory, which burnt up in the atmosphere on Thursday after decades of service.

Matt Williams

Senior International Editor

item.title: Why the Cambridge Analytica scandal still matters
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Meta’s $25B fine left out accountability for harm from the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal • 70 years ago the Suez crisis exposed British relative decline. Today, the Iran conflict could be doing the same for the US • Some states are stepping up after federal childcare cuts – and now offer lessons for the future • How to prepare your online life for your death • Not in a FEMA flood zone? Your home could still be at risk – and you could suffer more than your neighbor • Does time on social media make teens anxious and depressed? The evidence is not so clear
item.content:encoded:
As of the writing of this newsletter, the results of the U.S. midterm elections have not yet come in. But whatever the outcome, the shadow of a near-decade-old scandal involving tech giant Meta and Cambridge Analytica, a U.K. firm that worked for the 2016 Trump campaign, is likely to keep hanging over American politics.

Meta faces a legal penalty of US$25 billion over deception about data privacy, one of the largest such fines ever. But the full truth about Cambridge Analytica may never be known, according to Emma L. Briant of the University of Notre Dame. She argues that the deal failed to address the question of how much harm was caused when Cambridge Analytica used Facebook users’ data without their knowledge to influence voting behavior – and what Meta should have done to prevent the abuse.

A scholar of information warfare, Briant cites a series of bungled investigations and Meta’s aggressive stonewalling. She also points out that another recent Meta settlement – this one involving child safety – included little-noticed language that released all Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by the 47 participating U.S. states in the lawsuit.

A long history of “settlements and releases have meant the company paid a relatively small price for its deception while not having the harms from the data exploitation adjudicated,” she writes.

Helen Fessenden

Senior Economy and Business Editor, The Conversation U.S.

Meta’s $25B fine left out accountability for harm from the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal

A New Mexico judge’s fine hit Meta for deception about the data privacy violations, not for the harm they caused. A researcher who helped uncover the scandal explains.

We were surprised to find only a very weak link between the time they spent on social media and their levels of anxiety and depression. This suggests simply restricting young people’s access to social media ... may be missing the broader picture.

item.title: A midterm election with real meaning
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Are American voters actually gloomy about the economy, or is something else going on? • Nearly all Americans believe corruption is a problem. But will it decide the midterm elections? • I’ve been talking to MAGA supporters for years – here’s why some are sticking with Trump • How the Sphinx is helping answer a riddle about extinct crocodiles • Human speech follows the same patterns as birdsong — new research
item.content:encoded:
This will be the fifth U.S. midterm election that I have experienced as a resident alien in America – a position that affords me a decent perch as an outside observer, if not as a voter. And while I’m sure those past four midterms seemed pretty pivotal at the time, this one does feels a little different.

First up, a lot appears to be at stake. A Democrat “wave” – much predicted over here in the run-up to today’s vote – could see Donald Trump left as the lamest of lame ducks, forced to navigate his last two years in office with an oppositionist House and Senate bent on thwarting his policies.

So what is motivating Americans as they head to the ballot box? Well, the adage of it being “the economy, stupid” rings true(ish) – but in a slightly odd way. As politics and inequality expert Erin Lockwood explains, many of the fundamentals of the U.S. economy are pretty decent – GDP growth, employment and investment are all relatively healthy. Yet consumer sentiment is very low, and inflation alone can’t fully explain this gloom. Lockwood suggests that instead, the downbeat vibes are “driven by concerns over income and wealth that conventional measures don’t fully capture.”

Another takeaway is that this feeling of economic malaise is shared by Republican- and Democrat-leaning Americans alike, bucking a trend that usually sees voters’ perception of the economy shaped by whether their party is in power. Americans also find bipartisan consensus on another issue: corruption. U.S. studies researcher Jared Mondschein notes that polling shows 80%-plus support for the belief that “government corruption is widespread” among Republicans, Democrats and independents. And this has translated into campaign ads that seek to portray candidates as outsiders, rather than part of the party faithful.

“Americans have largely been against Washington insiders for decades – particularly when economic anxiety is high,” Mondschein notes. He adds: “Yet what’s different in this year’s midterm elections is how many are trying to fuse corruption with that economic anxiety. Not since the 2006 midterm elections has corruption been such a prominent theme in an election.”

So, with anti-incumbent, gloomy voters expected to give Republicans a bit of a bloody nose, who is sticking with Trump’s brand of conservatism? Anthropologist Alex Hinton sought to find out by attending a series of MAGA rallies in the lead-up to the midterm elections. He identified three key themes as to why the Trump faithful remain so: fear of socialism, support for the president’s immigration policy, and a belief that despite the current economic ill winds, Trump is the man to navigate the U.S. through the doldrums.

Just how far that committed base can mitigate what is expected to be a pretty damning midterm verdict on Trump’s agenda may become clearer later today when the vote counts start coming in.

Matt Williams

Senior International Editor

Top story

Economic pessimism among Americans in both political parties is deepening ahead of the November midterm elections, amid factors such as high energy prices and cost-of-living pressures. AP Photo/Jeff Chiu

Are American voters actually gloomy about the economy, or is something else going on?

Erin Kay Lockwood, University of California, Irvine

Many standard measures of economic health are strong, but voters in both parties are increasingly pessimistic.

Nearly all Americans believe corruption is a problem. But will it decide the midterm elections?

Jared Mondschein, University of Sydney

The vast majority of Americans believe government corruption is widespread – both Democrats and Republicans. Politicians have taken notice.

I’ve been talking to MAGA supporters for years – here’s why some are sticking with Trump

Alex Hinton, Rutgers University - Newark

Despite the headwinds that have cratered support for Donald Trump – high prices, the Iran war, corruption – many of Trump’s MAGA loyalists still back him. A scholar who studies MAGA looks at why.

How the Sphinx is helping answer a riddle about extinct crocodiles

Philip Mannion, UCL

New technology is helping to identify extinct fossil species.

Human speech follows the same patterns as birdsong — new research

Logan S. James, McGill University; The University of Texas at Austin; Jon Sakata, McGill University; Kendra Oudyk, University of British Columbia

A new study compares the songs of 367 bird species with song and speech from 52 human languages to reveal shared acoustic patterns.

item.title: Anthropic's IPO and stock market risk
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us • PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat • People are using AI to make expensive computer programs free. This could change everything • Made in China AI: new tech, same old story? • As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s upcoming entry into the stock market, which it signaled this week by filing paperwork for an initial public offering, is going to make some people a lot of money. For retail investors, though, the high concentration of AI companies in the stock market means that regular people’s investments are exposed to AI-related risks, writes a finance scholar.

Large language models are rapidly reshaping the software industry, as two stories demonstrate this week. The technology was instrumental in identifying a vulnerability in PHP, a language used in millions of websites, and the technology’s ability to reverse engineer existing software packages could upend pricing in the commercial market for apps.

Also this week, a look at whether China’s push into AI will follow the same economic path as other technologies, and what happens to human workers’ skills as they hand off more and more to AI.

Martin LaMonica

Director of Editorial Projects and Newsletters

Webinar

Lead story

Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us

Marta Khomyn, Adelaide University

This is the first time a company has come to market warning of ‘catastrophic or existential risks to humanity’.

If consumer and business demand for AI disappoints, tech companies’ bond prices and credit ratings would likely fall together – just as their shares would.

Cybersecurity

PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat

Doug Jacobson, Iowa State University

A cybersecurity researcher explains how a flaw in widespread software makes millions of websites vulnerable to hackers – and underscores the role of AI in attacking and defending the internet.

Business

People are using AI to make expensive computer programs free. This could change everything

Dana McKay, RMIT University

Some say this will take us back to the cool, weird internet of the 1990s.

Made in China AI: new tech, same old story?

Iordanis Kalaitzoglou, Audencia

History could repeat itself if China turns AI into an abundant, commodity-driven industry. Should we be worried about AI’s new land of plenty?

Work

As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?

Murugan Anandarajan, Drexel University

Having a human “in the loop” overseeing when an AI makes a decision is important, but what happens to that responsible human over time when the AI gets it right over and over again?

item.title: From psephology to spook-ology
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Israel has voted, but what comes next? Dissecting a messy ballot and coalition-building process • Werewolf mice, ghostly frogs and zombie cockroaches: the animal versions of our Halloween horrors • Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon-stealing spirits • Buried cats, exorcisms and a sunken Colonel Sanders – the strange world of sporting curses • The female scream is now an all-powerful cry in horror films • I’ve been talking to MAGA supporters for years, and here’s why some are sticking with Trump — and others are not • Who mapped Africa? Debunking the myth that Europeans alone plotted the continent • Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or – a victory for sportsmanship over celebrity
item.content:encoded:
Over the last few days, voters have opted for continuity in Brazil, change in Serbia, and in Israel … well, that is going to take some time to work out.

But today’s newsletter is more about otherworldly matters than global concerns. You see, us editors at The Conversation love Halloween – it is a chance to scour the academic world for research on all things spooky and scary. Take zoologists Alex Dittrich and Kat Hamill’s deep dive into the world of animals that display behaviors common to your favorite horror characters. Here we find cannibal mice that howl at the moon, wasps with the ability to turn prey into zombies and ghostly translucent frogs.

Meanwhile, Vaughan Cruickshank takes a look at how buried cats and spurned goats have contributed to cursed teams and sporting failure. And for those who love a good jump scare, culture scholars Sara Beth Lyons and James Deaville, explore what goes into a good movie scream and how the art of the shriek has evolved over the decades.

Finally, Marcus Librizzi – who collects ghost stories from around the world – explains the deeper meaning to the genre. “These stories can keep alive the memory of a dark past. In my research I have come across tales that preserve memories of injustices that might otherwise have been forgotten,” he writes.

Matt Williams

Senior International Editor

Top story

Gadi Eisenkot or Benjamin Netanyahu – under whose direction will Israel head? Erik Marmor/picture alliance via Getty Images

Israel has voted, but what comes next? Dissecting a messy ballot and coalition-building process

Dov Waxman, University of California, Los Angeles

With no clear majority for the ruling coalition or main opposition bloc, working out who will form the next government could take months.

They have creepy tendencies but these animals are real not fictional.

Medieval ghost stories featured rotten flesh, the walking dead and spoon-stealing spirits

Alex Brown, Durham University

Medieval ghosts shapeshifted, rose from their graves, and begged for help in making amends for their misdeeds.

Buried cats, exorcisms and a sunken Colonel Sanders – the strange world of sporting curses

Vaughan Cruickshank, University of Tasmania

Why would fans of a Japanese baseball team throw a statue of Colonel Sanders into a local canal? Welcome to the world of sporting curses.

The female scream is now an all-powerful cry in horror films

James Deaville, Carleton University; Sara Beth Lyons, Carleton University

As Halloween approaches and horror movies circulate, a look at the legendary ‘scream queens’ and their talent and power.

Non-spooky stories

I’ve been talking to MAGA supporters for years, and here’s why some are sticking with Trump — and others are not

Alex Hinton, Rutgers University - Newark

Despite the headwinds that have cratered support for Donald Trump – high prices, the Iran war, corruption – many of Trump’s MAGA loyalists still back him. A scholar who studies MAGA looks at why.

Who mapped Africa? Debunking the myth that Europeans alone plotted the continent

Thomas J Bassett, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

African guides drew lines in the sand to help Europeans understand the terrain. But they rarely got the credit.

Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or – a victory for sportsmanship over celebrity

Josh Bland, University of Cambridge

Harry Kane represents a hard grafting and unshowy sportsmanship many would like to see as the future of football.

    Brooke N. Newman, Virginia Commonwealth University

    For locals, the king’s Caribbean visit is an occasion to recognize the full story of Britain’s trafficking and enslavement of millions of people across the Atlantic.

  • Indonesia’s El Niño-driven peat fires are choking the region – and releasing centuries of stored carbon

    Gareth Roberts, University of Southampton; Martin Wooster, King's College London

    An intense drought is the match. Decades of deforestation and peat draining provide the fuel.

  • Serbia’s leaderless student movement has won a historic election – but what happens next?

    Eric Gordy, UCL

    With no leader or political experience, Serbia’s student movement now begins talks to form a government.

  • EU’s new Arctic strategy signals shift in its geopolitical mindset

    Emilie Canova, University of Cambridge; Centre national de la recherche scientifique (CNRS)

    The EU has unveiled its first Arctic strategy since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

  • Private equity is buying up more methadone clinics – access to the lifesaving drug isn’t getting easier

    Yashaswini Singh, Brown University

    Despite acquiring more than one-third of US methadone clinics, private equity has not significantly expanded methadone availability.

  • How porn became so extreme – and how it’s shaping the sex lives of young people

    Gemma Ware, The Conversation

    Extreme pornography has become readily available on mainstream porn sites. Clare McGlynn explains what this is doing to the sex lives of young people.

item.title: Why voters don't respond to promises of cash
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work • Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us • We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth • Victorian spiritualism capitalised on the desire to transcend death to create new ways of making money • Halloween meets history in many ghostly tourism attractions. Is this a problem? • Daylight saving was meant to save energy. Do we still need it in the age of LEDs?
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has a long history of offering money to voters – a recent example being his pledge of US$5,000 to every American if Republicans win the November 2026 midterm elections.

His Republican allies in Congress didn’t take action on the proposal, which would cost over $1 trillion. But these cash promises are one thing that Trump has in common with many politicians, past and present, all around the world. Vote buying, in fact, goes back to ancient Rome.

The puzzle is why party leaders still think this is such a good idea, writes Kenneth Greene, a political scientist at the University of Texas-Austin. His research, which looks at vote buying globally but focuses in particular on Mexico, concludes that this practice almost never pays off.

As he explains, whatever cash incentive a party offers has to outweigh a person’s desire to vote their actual preferences – a tall order. It’s also hard for party machines to identify the “right” swing voter, and just as hard to ensure.

There’s also one major downside for democracy, notes Greene. A party may triumph at the polls, but it will never know whether it won because voters believed in its platform or because they expected to get paid.

Helen Fessenden

Senior Economy and Business Editor, The Conversation U.S.

Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work

Kenneth Greene, The University of Texas at Austin

Money or other material benefits are often not enough to override a voter’s preferences and partisanship.

Essential briefings

Anthropic’s record US$2 trillion stock market listing highlights the growing risks for all of us

Marta Khomyn, Adelaide University

This is the first time a company has come to market warning of ‘catastrophic or existential risks to humanity’.

We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth

Simon Buechler, Miami University; Lyndsey Rolheiser, York University, Canada

This employment boost took three to five years to show up, two researchers found after studying more than two decades of data.

Victorian spiritualism capitalised on the desire to transcend death to create new ways of making money

James Cronin, Lancaster University; Sophie James, Lancaster University

The very technologies that transformed Victorian commerce and entertainment also helped make ghosts visible, reproducible and profitable.

Halloween meets history in many ghostly tourism attractions. Is this a problem?

Ann-Kathrin McLean, Royal Roads University; Juan Claudio Benavides del Carpio, Royal Roads University

All attractions situated along a ‘dark tourism spectrum’ must carefully navigate questions about respectful engagement and exploitation.

Quote of the week

The original justification for daylight saving time as an energy-saving measure is increasingly uncertain. Broadly, research suggests reductions in lighting demand are most likely to be balanced by increased heating and cooling demand. Any energy savings are likely to be relatively small and depend on factors beyond lighting efficiency.

—

Amin Al-Habaibeh, Professor of Intelligent Engineering Systems, Nottingham Trent University

Daylight saving was meant to save energy. Do we still need it in the age of LEDs?

Technology

  • Shares in this data centre company are down 40% as investors lose faith in the AI story

    Andrew Cullen, The University of Melbourne

    While AI hype is strong, the business models are coming under increasing scrutiny.

  • How should AI be regulated? Follow the harm

    Sylvia Lu, American University

    Instead of trying to restrict AI technologies, regulations could focus on the harm the technology causes people and companies.

  • Data centers are inspiring bipartisanship – for now

    Barbara A. Trish, Grinnell College

    A political scientist who studies AI in campaigns explains why data centers have put Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon on the same side ahead of the midterms.

  • AI chatbots can be a valuable health resource for older adults – if they embrace ‘informed skepticism’

    Robin Brewer, University of Michigan

    AI can help you navigate health information, but evaluating the credibility and quality of responses is key.

Personal finance

  • The psychology that can lead investors to make bad financial decisions

    Donald Amuah, University of South Wales

    Recent research suggests even people training for careers in finance can fall prey to overconfidence, loss aversion and other psychological biases.

Economy

  • How El Niño could push up your mortgage and grocery bills

    Narmin Nahidi, University of Exeter

    A Pacific climate event has far reaching effects.

  • Zimbabwe wants digital payments to build trust in its newest currency. Why technology alone won’t be enough to save the ZiG

    Jonathan Munemo, Salisbury University

    Zimbabwe’s goal should be to promote wider adoption of the local currency, not to use technology to force it.

item.title: Voters make their mark
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.description: • Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track • ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power • Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics • Palestinian citizens face a painful choice in Israel’s election: To vote or not
item.content:encoded:
A big week for elections got off to a bang on Sunday when Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback to win Brazil’s presidential poll, beating rightwing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro by a whisker. Lula gained 51.79 per cent of votes against 48.21 per cent for the son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, in a two-way run-off in Latin America’s largest democracy.

As Guilherme Casarões points out, now comes the hard part for the 80-year-old Lula as he starts his fourth term in office.

On Monday it was Serbia’s turn. A grassroots Student List won up to 140 of the Serbian parliament’s 250 seats, marking a dramatic defeat for strongman and nationalist president Aleksandar Vučić. Gavin Brent Sullivan and Tereza Capelos explain the Student List’s remarkable story.

And today Israel goes to the polls in an election that will have consequences beyond the country’s borders. Hannah Ridge unpacks why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway while Tamir Sorek explains the painful choice faced by Palestinian citizens - whether to vote, or whether to boycott the poll.

Caroline Southey

Founding Editor, Africa

Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track

Guilherme Casarões, Florida International University

The real antidote to polarisation will not come from a single election or a single leader.

‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power

Gavin Brent Sullivan, International Psychoanalytic University Berlin; Tereza Capelos, University of Southampton

A record number of voters turned out to end Alexander Vučić’s longstanding dominance of Serbian politics.

Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics

Hannah Ridge, Chapman University; Institute for Humane Studies

Ultra-Orthodox Jews, often called Haredim, make up a small but growing percentage of Israel’s population. Still, their political parties wield significant influence.

Palestinian citizens face a painful choice in Israel’s election: To vote or not

Tamir Sorek, Penn State

More than a third of Israel’s Palestinian citizens are expected to sit out the election.

  • UN peacekeepers prepare to exit Lebanon after 70 years – leaving behind a worrying security vacuum

    Mireille Rebeiz, Dickinson College; University of Otago

    In August, the UN Security Council voted to end the decades-long peacekeeping mission in Lebanon. Blue helmets will leave by the end of the year.

  • PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat

    Doug Jacobson, Iowa State University

    A cybersecurity researcher explains how a flaw in widespread software makes millions of websites vulnerable to hackers – and underscores the role of AI in attacking and defending the internet.

  • Stanford prison experiment: why do controversial psychology studies still have such a hold on us?

    David Kaposi, The Open University

    A new Netflix series has revived interest in the Stanford prison experiment. Zimbardo and Milgram’s flawed studies still leave a question unanswered.

  • Why do people still get polio in some countries and not in others?

    Katrine L. Wallace, University of Illinois Chicago

    Polio can survive only where it finds kids who aren’t protected by a vaccine.
